content: 1. The second postnatal contact should occur on the third day after childbirth, approximately 48 to 72 hours postpartum. 2. The third postnatal contact should take place between the seventh and fourteenth day after childbirth. 3. The final postnatal contact, typically a clinic visit, should be scheduled at six weeks postpartum. During this visit, your baby will receive vaccinations, and it is essential to ensure your baby is immunized. When to seek care for danger signs: 4. If you experience increased vaginal bleeding, seizures, rapid or difficult breathing, fever with extreme weakness preventing you from getting out of bed, severe headaches accompanied by blurred vision, or calf pain with redness or swelling, you must go to the hospital or health center immediately, day or night. Do not wait. 5. If you notice swollen, red, or tender breasts or nipples, difficulty urinating or urinary leakage, increased pain or signs of infection in the perineum, infection at the wound site, or foul-smelling vaginal discharge, visit the health center as soon as possible. Self-care after an abortion: 6. Rest for a few days if you feel tired. 7. Light vaginal bleeding, similar to menstrual bleeding or spotting, is normal for several weeks after an abortion. 8. Some pain is expected as the uterus contracts. Mild painkillers can help alleviate cramping pain, but if the pain worsens over time, seek medical attention. 9. Avoid sexual intercourse or inserting anything into the vagina until the bleeding stops. 10. Practice safe sex and use condoms correctly during every sexual act if at risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or HIV. 11. Follow up with your healthcare provider as instructed. Family planning after an abortion: 12. Remember that you can become pregnant as soon as you resume sexual activity. Use a family planning method to prevent unwanted pregnancy. Danger signs after an abortion: 13. Seek immediate care if you experience increased or prolonged bleeding for more than two days, fever, feeling unwell, dizziness or fainting, abdominal pain, backache, nausea, vomiting, or foul-smelling vaginal discharge. Care for the newborn: 14. Wash your baby’s face and neck daily, and bathe them as needed. After bathing, dry the baby thoroughly, dress them, and keep them warm. 15. Clean the baby’s bottom when soiled and dry it thoroughly. 16. Wash your hands with soap and water before and after handling your baby, especially after touching their bottom. Umbilical cord care: 17. Keep the cord stump loosely covered with a clean cloth. Fold diapers and clothes below the stump. 18. Do not apply any substances to the stump. If the birth occurred at home without a skilled attendant, apply chlorhexidine to the stump daily until it separates. 19. If the stump area becomes soiled, wash it with clean water and soap, then dry it completely with a clean cloth. 20. Wash your hands with soap and water before and after caring for the cord. Keeping the newborn warm: 21. In cold climates, ensure at least one area of the room is warm. 22. Newborns require more clothing than older children or adults. If the baby feels cold, place a hat on their head and cover them with an extra blanket during cold nights. Breastfeeding: 23. For the first six months of life, the baby needs only breast milk—no water, other milk, cereals, teas, or juices. 24. Breast milk provides all the water and nutrients a baby needs, is easily digested, and protects against infections and allergies while supporting growth and development. 25. Breastfeeding benefits the mother by reducing postpartum bleeding through uterine contractions stimulated by the baby’s sucking and delaying the return of fertility. Suggestions for successful breastfeeding: 26. Keep your baby close to you immediately after birth, either in your bed or within easy reach. 27. Begin breastfeeding within one hour of birth. 28. The baby’s sucking stimulates milk production; the more the baby feeds, the more milk you will produce. 29. Allow the baby to feed and release one breast before offering the second. Alternate breasts at each feeding. 30. Give your baby the first milk (colostrum), which is rich in nutrients and antibodies to protect their health. 31. At night, keep your baby close to you for easy access to breastfeeding. 32. Drink plenty of clean, safe water while breastfeeding. Health worker support for breastfeeding: 33. A health worker can help you correctly position the baby and ensure proper attachment to the breast, reducing breast problems. 34. They can teach you how to express milk by hand if you need to leave the baby with another caregiver for short periods. 35. They can connect you with a breastfeeding support group. 36. If you encounter any difficulties with breastfeeding, seek help from a health worker immediately. Breastfeeding and family planning: 37. Exclusive breastfeeding, day and night, for the first six months postpartum, along with the absence of menstruation, provides protection against pregnancy. Clean home delivery: 38. Regardless of the delivery location, it is strongly recommended that all women deliver with a skilled attendant. 39. If delivering at home, ensure the attendant and family members are aware of the emergency plan and danger signs for both mother and baby. 40. Arrange for a support person to assist the attendant and stay with you during labor and after delivery. 41. Prepare a clean, warm birth area with fresh air and a light source. 42. Have clean supplies ready, including a new razor blade, three pieces of string (20 cm each) to tie the cord, and clean cloths for covering the birth area. Instructions for a clean and safe home delivery: 43. Ensure a clean delivery surface for the baby’s birth. 44. Ask the attendant to wash their hands before touching you or the baby, with short and clean nails. 45. After birth, place the baby on your abdomen or chest to keep them warm and clean. Dry the baby thoroughly and cover them with a clean, dry cloth. 46. Cut the cord when it stops pulsating, using a disposable delivery kit as instructed. 47. Wait for the placenta to deliver naturally. 48. Keep yourself and your baby warm, with the baby dressed or wrapped and their head covered with a cap. 49. Begin breastfeeding within the first hour of birth when the baby shows readiness. Avoid harmful practices during delivery: 50. Do not use local medications to hasten labor. 51. Do not wait for the waters to stop before going to a health facility. 52. Do not insert any substances into the vagina during or after labor. 53. Do not push on the abdomen during labor or delivery. 54. Do not pull on the cord to deliver the placenta. 55. Do not apply ashes, cow dung, or other substances to the umbilical cord or stump. Encourage helpful traditional practices: 56. Promote practices that support clean and safe delivery and postpartum care. Danger signs during delivery: 57. For the mother: Seek immediate care if the waters break and labor does not start within six hours, labor pains last more than 12 hours, heavy bleeding occurs (soaking more than 2–3 pads in 15 minutes), or the placenta is not expelled within one hour after the baby’s birth. 58. For the baby: Seek immediate care if the baby is very small, has difficulty breathing, seizures, fever, feels cold, is bleeding, or cannot feed. Routine postnatal contacts: 59. If the birth occurs at home, the first postnatal contact should be within 24 hours of birth. 60. The second contact should occur on day three (48–72 hours postpartum). 61. The third contact should take place between days seven and fourteen postpartum. Care during pregnancy: 62. Visit a health worker as soon as you suspect you are pregnant to begin care early. 63. During visits, the health worker will monitor your health and pregnancy progress, help you create a birth plan, answer questions, provide treatment for conditions like malaria and anemia, and administer tetanus immunizations. 64. Follow advice on breastfeeding, birth spacing, nutrition, HIV counseling and testing, and other health matters. 65. Bring your maternal health record to every visit. Self-care during pregnancy: 66. Eat a healthy diet with more fruits, vegetables, beans, meat, fish, eggs, cheese, and milk. 67. Take iron tablets and other prescribed supplements or medications daily. 68. Rest when possible and avoid lifting heavy objects. 69. Sleep under an insecticide-treated bed net. 70. Do not take medications unless prescribed by a health worker. 71. Avoid alcohol and smoking. 72. Use condoms correctly during every sexual act to prevent STIs or HIV if at risk. Danger signs during pregnancy: 73. Seek immediate care if you experience painful contractions every 20 minutes or less, your bag of water breaks, or you have bloody, sticky discharge. 74. Do not wait if you have vaginal bleeding, convulsions, severe headaches with blurred vision, fever with extreme weakness, severe abdominal pain, or fast or difficult breathing. Preparing a birth and emergency plan: 75. Discuss and review your birth plan at every health center visit. 76. Plan for delivery with a skilled attendant, whether at a hospital, health center, or home. 77. Organize a clean and warm delivery area, a maternal health record, and a clean delivery kit with essential supplies.
